text: I have shewed you all things, how that so labouring ye ought to support the weak, and to remember the words of the Lord Jesus, how he said, It is more blessed to give than to receive.
reflection: Paul was saying goodbye to the leaders of the church in Ephesus. He knew he would likely never see them again. As he reminded them how he had lived among them, working with his own hands to support himself and others, he quoted words of Jesus not recorded anywhere else: "It is more blessed to give than to receive." Our culture often teaches the opposite. Happiness is found in getting more. But Jesus turns that upside down. Real blessing is found in giving. Those who have experienced generosity know this is true. There is a joy in giving that receiving cannot match. It frees us from the grip of possessions. It connects us to others. It reflects the heart of God, the greatest Giver of all. Paul also mentions supporting the weak. Giving is not just about money. It includes time, attention, help, and care for those who cannot repay. This month we will think about generosity and good works. Begin by discovering the blessing of giving.
question: How could you discover the joy of giving in some way today?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You said it is more blessed to give than to receive. Free me from always wanting more, and let me find real blessing in giving today. Amen.

text: Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.
reflection: Paul was collecting a gift for poor believers in Jerusalem, and he wrote to the Corinthians about how to give. His instruction was clear: "Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." Notice three things. First, giving is personal: as he purposeth in his heart. It is a decision each person makes before God. Second, it should not be grudging or forced. Giving that comes from pressure or guilt misses the point. Third, God loves a cheerful giver. The word cheerful has the sense of glad and joyful. God is not mainly interested in the size of our gifts. He cares about the heart behind them. A small gift given gladly delights Him more than a large one given with a frown. Cheerful giving comes from understanding how much God has given us. When we remember His generosity, our own giving becomes a joy. Give gladly today.
question: Is there a gift you have been giving grudgingly that you could give gladly instead?
prayer: Lord, You love a cheerful giver, and You have been so generous to me. Take away any grudging spirit, and let me give gladly from a thankful heart. Amen.

text: But this I say, He which soweth sparingly shall reap also sparingly; and he which soweth bountifully shall reap also bountifully.
reflection: Every farmer knows a basic truth. If you plant a few seeds, you get a small harvest. If you plant many, you get a large one. Paul applies that principle to generosity: "He which soweth sparingly shall reap also sparingly; and he which soweth bountifully shall reap also bountifully." This is not a formula for getting rich. Paul is not saying that if you give money, God will automatically give you more money. The harvest he describes is broader. A few verses later, he says God will make all grace abound toward you, so that you will have enough for every good work. The return on generosity includes joy, gratitude, deeper faith, strengthened relationships, and the ability to give even more. Generous people tend to live generous lives in every way. Stingy people tend to live small lives. What kind of sowing are you doing? Not only with money, but with kindness, time, and encouragement. Sow bountifully today.
question: Where could you sow generously today with your time, kindness, or resources?
prayer: Lord, help me sow bountifully and not sparingly. Let me be generous with my time, my kindness, and what I have, and trust You for the harvest. Amen.

text: Give, and it shall be given unto you; good measure, pressed down, and shaken together, and running over, shall men give into your bosom. For with the same measure that ye mete withal it shall be measured to you again.
reflection: Jesus used a picture from the marketplace. When buying grain, a generous seller would fill the container, press it down to make room, shake it to settle it, and keep pouring until it ran over the top. Jesus said that is how giving comes back to us: "Give, and it shall be given unto you; good measure, pressed down, and shaken together, and running over." Then He added a principle: "For with the same measure that ye mete withal it shall be measured to you again." This verse comes right after Jesus' teaching on judging and forgiving. So it applies to more than money. The measure we use for mercy, forgiveness, kindness, and generosity tends to return to us. Those who are generous with grace find grace overflowing in their lives. Those who are stingy with others often find life feels stingy too. God is not stingy. He gives in overflowing measure. Today, let your measure toward others be generous, pressed down, and running over.
question: In what way, besides money, could you be generous with someone today?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You promised good measure, pressed down and running over. Make me generous with mercy, kindness, and patience, as well as with what I own. Amen.

text: The liberal soul shall be made fat: and he that watereth shall be watered also himself.
reflection: Proverbs gives a picture of refreshment: "The liberal soul shall be made fat: and he that watereth shall be watered also himself." Liberal here means generous. To be made fat in that culture meant to prosper, to be well nourished and satisfied. The generous person is not drained by giving. They are enriched. And the second half paints a lovely image. The one who waters others will himself be watered. Imagine someone carrying water to thirsty plants on a hot day. As they work, they are splashed and cooled themselves. Refreshing others refreshes us. Many people discover this. When they are feeling low, helping someone else lifts their own spirits. When they are worried about their own needs, giving to others reminds them that God provides. Generosity breaks the grip of self-focus. If you feel dry today, try watering someone else. Encourage them, help them, or meet a need. You may find yourself refreshed in the process.
question: If you feel dry today, whom could you refresh with encouragement or help?
prayer: Lord, the one who waters others shall be watered also. If I feel dry, help me pour out encouragement to someone else, and refresh me as I do. Amen.

text: He that hath pity upon the poor lendeth unto the LORD; and that which he hath given will he pay him again.
reflection: Proverbs makes an astonishing claim about helping the poor: "He that hath pity upon the poor lendeth unto the LORD; and that which he hath given will he pay him again." When we help someone in need, we are not just giving to them. We are lending to God. The Creator of the universe takes it personally. He considers Himself indebted. And God always repays His debts. This changes how we see generosity toward the poor. It is not wasted. It is not lost. It is an investment in God's own hands. And He is the most faithful debtor there is. His repayment may not always come in the form we expect. It may come as provision, peace, joy, or eternal reward. But it will come. Jesus later said something similar: whatever we do for the least of these, we do for Him. Today, look for someone in need. Show them compassion. And know that you are lending to the Lord.
question: Who in need could you show compassion to today, knowing God takes it personally?
prayer: Lord, showing pity to the poor is lending to You. Thank You that no kindness to the needy is wasted. Show me someone I can help today. Amen.

text: Honour the LORD with thy substance, and with the firstfruits of all thine increase…
reflection: In ancient Israel, the first part of every harvest was set aside for God. Before the farmer used any of the crop for himself, he brought the firstfruits as an offering. Proverbs teaches this principle: "Honour the LORD with thy substance, and with the firstfruits of all thine increase." Firstfruits means the first and best, not the leftovers. Giving God our firstfruits is a statement of trust. It says, God comes first, and I believe He will provide for the rest. It is easy to give God what is left over after everything else is paid. But that often means very little is left. Putting Him first changes the order of our priorities. This principle applies beyond money. We can give God the first part of our day in prayer, the first moments of a decision in seeking His will, and our best energy in serving Him. Today, think about what it would look like to give God your firstfruits. Honour Him with your best.
question: Are you giving God your first and best, or what is left over?
prayer: Lord, I want to honour You with my substance and the firstfruits of all I have. Help me give You my first and best as a statement of trust in You. Amen.

text: Withhold not good from them to whom it is due, when it is in the power of thine hand to do it.
reflection: Sometimes the hardest part of doing good is simply doing it now. Proverbs addresses that: "Withhold not good from them to whom it is due, when it is in the power of thine hand to do it." The next verse adds, do not say to your neighbour, go, and come again, and tomorrow I will give, when you have it with you. Delay is a quiet way of withholding. We mean to help. We intend to call, visit, or encourage. But we put it off, and the moment passes. This verse also speaks of good that is due. Some good is owed: wages to workers, debts to lenders, honour to parents, gratitude to those who helped us. Withholding what is owed is a form of injustice. And notice the phrase: when it is in the power of thine hand. If you can do good now, do it. Is there something good you have been meaning to do? A payment, a thank-you, a visit, or a helping hand? Do not wait. Do it today.
question: What good have you been meaning to do that you could do today?
prayer: Lord, keep me from withholding good when it is in my power to do it. Forgive my delays, and help me do the good I have been putting off today. Amen.

text: Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house, and prove me now herewith, saith the LORD of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it.
reflection: In Malachi's day, God's people had become careless in their giving. They were holding back what they owed, and the work of God's house suffered. So God issued a remarkable challenge: "prove me now herewith, saith the LORD of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it." This is one of the few places in Scripture where God invites His people to test Him. Prove me. Try Me. See if I will not be faithful. God was not asking for their money because He needed it. He was inviting them to trust Him. Holding back came from fear that there would not be enough. God answered that fear with a promise of overflowing blessing. Generosity is ultimately a matter of trust. Do we believe God will provide if we give? The windows of heaven are not opened by stinginess. Trust Him with your giving today.
question: Where is fear of not having enough holding back your giving?
prayer: Lord, You invited Your people to prove You and see the windows of heaven opened. Help me trust You to provide, and let that trust free me to give. Amen.

text: And he called unto him his disciples, and saith unto them, Verily I say unto you, That this poor widow hath cast more in, than all they which have cast into the treasury…
reflection: Jesus sat near the temple treasury, watching people give. Many wealthy people put in large amounts. Then a poor widow came and dropped in two tiny copper coins, worth almost nothing. Jesus called His disciples over and said, "Verily I say unto you, That this poor widow hath cast more in, than all they which have cast into the treasury." How could two small coins be more than all the large gifts? Jesus explained: the rich gave out of their abundance, but she gave out of her poverty. She gave all she had to live on. God does not measure gifts by their size. He measures them by their sacrifice and the heart behind them. The rich gave what they would not miss. The widow gave what she could not spare. This story encourages anyone who feels their gift is too small to matter. In God's eyes, it may be the greatest gift of all. Give what you can today, with your whole heart.
question: What could you give today with your whole heart, however small it seems?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You saw the widow's two mites and called them more than all the rest. Thank You that You measure the heart, not the size. Help me give what I can wholeheartedly. Amen.

text: But when thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth…
reflection: In Jesus' day, some people made a show of their giving. They wanted everyone to see how generous they were. Jesus said they already had their reward: the applause of people. Then He gave a different instruction: "But when thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth." It is a vivid picture. Give so quietly that even your other hand does not notice. Do not keep a mental record of your generosity. Do not draw attention to it. Simply give and move on. Why? Because the motive matters. If we give to be seen, we have already received what we wanted. But if we give quietly, out of love for God and others, our Father who sees in secret will reward us. Social media can make this harder. It is tempting to share every good deed. But there is a special joy in doing good that no one else knows about. Today, do something generous in secret. Let it be just between you and God.
question: What generous thing could you do in secret today, for God's eyes only?
prayer: Father, You see in secret. Free me from the need to be noticed, and let me give quietly today, trusting that You see and that Your reward is enough. Amen.

text: Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven.
reflection: Just a few chapters before warning against showy giving, Jesus said something that may seem to contradict it: "Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven." Should our good works be hidden or seen? The answer is in the motive and the goal. When we give to be praised ourselves, Jesus says hide it. But our lives as a whole should shine in a way that points people to God. The difference is where the glory goes. Showy giving draws attention to us. Shining light draws attention to the Father. A light is not meant to be admired for itself. It is meant to help people see. When our kindness, honesty, and generosity are visible in daily life, others notice. And when done with humility, they may wonder where it comes from. That is when they glorify God. Today, let your light shine through ordinary good works, and let the glory go to Him.
question: How could an ordinary good work today point someone toward God instead of toward you?
prayer: Father, let my light so shine that others may see my good works and glorify You. Let my life point people to You, not to myself. Amen.

text: And the King shall answer and say unto them, Verily I say unto you, Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.
reflection: Jesus described a scene of final judgment. The King separates people as a shepherd separates sheep from goats. To those on His right, He says, I was hungry and you fed me, thirsty and you gave me drink, a stranger and you took me in. They are puzzled. When did we do that? And the King answers, "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me." Jesus identifies with the least. The hungry, the thirsty, the stranger, the sick, and the prisoner. When we serve them, we serve Him. This changes how we see every person in need. The homeless man, the lonely neighbour, the struggling family, the person in the hospital bed. In serving them, we are serving Christ. Notice that the righteous did not even realize it. Their kindness was not calculated. It was simply who they had become. Look for the least today. Serve them as if you are serving Jesus. Because you are.
question: Who among the least around you could you serve today as if serving Christ?
prayer: Lord Jesus, what I do for the least of these, I do for You. Open my eyes to the hungry, the stranger, the sick, and the lonely, and let me serve You through them. Amen.

text: And whosoever shall give to drink unto one of these little ones a cup of cold water only in the name of a disciple, verily I say unto you, he shall in no wise lose his reward.
reflection: Not all good works are big. Jesus pointed to one of the smallest acts of kindness imaginable: "whosoever shall give to drink unto one of these little ones a cup of cold water only in the name of a disciple, verily I say unto you, he shall in no wise lose his reward." A cup of cold water. In a hot, dry land, it was a real gift. But it costs almost nothing. Anyone can give it. And yet Jesus says it will not go unrewarded. God notices the smallest kindness. This should encourage anyone who feels they have little to offer. You may not be able to give large sums or start great ministries. But you can offer a cup of cold water. A smile, a word of encouragement, a meal for a tired neighbour, a few minutes of listening. These small things matter to God. None of them are forgotten. Today, look for a cup of cold water you can give. Small kindnesses add up to a life of love.
question: What simple kindness, like a cup of cold water, could you offer today?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You notice even a cup of cold water given in Your name. Help me not to overlook small kindnesses, and show me one I can offer today. Amen.

text: For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them.
reflection: Paul has just explained that salvation is God's gift, received by faith, not by our works. Then he adds this: "For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them." Good works are not the root of salvation. They are the fruit. We are not saved by good works, but we are saved for good works. The word workmanship can also mean masterpiece. You are God's handiwork, crafted with care. And He designed you with a purpose. Even more, He has prepared good works in advance for you to do. Before you were born, God had good things in mind for you to accomplish. That is a remarkable thought. Your life is not random. There are specific good works with your name on them, waiting for you to walk in them. Today, ask God to show you the good works He has prepared for you. Then step into them with joy.
question: What good work might God have prepared in advance for you to walk in today?
prayer: Lord, I am Your workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works. Show me the good works You have prepared for me today, and help me walk in them. Amen.

text: This is a faithful saying, and these things I will that thou affirm constantly, that they which have believed in God might be careful to maintain good works. These things are good and profitable unto men.
reflection: Paul wrote to Titus, a young leader on the island of Crete, with instructions for the churches there. After summarizing the gospel of grace, he said, "these things I will that thou affirm constantly, that they which have believed in God might be careful to maintain good works." Careful to maintain. The phrase suggests giving attention, taking thought, being intentional. Good works do not happen automatically. They need thought and planning. Maintain also suggests continuing, keeping them up, not letting them slide. Paul adds that these things are good and profitable unto men. Good works benefit others. They make a real difference in people's lives. Notice the connection: those who have believed in God. Faith leads to action. Those who truly trust God become people who do good. It is not optional decoration on the Christian life. It is part of its fabric. Today, be careful to maintain good works. Think ahead about how you can bless someone, and then follow through.
question: How could you think ahead today about blessing someone, and then follow through?
prayer: Lord, help me be careful to maintain good works. Give me thoughtfulness to plan how I can bless someone today, and faithfulness to follow through. Amen.

text: In all things shewing thyself a pattern of good works: in doctrine shewing uncorruptness, gravity, sincerity…
reflection: Paul gave Titus a personal challenge: "In all things shewing thyself a pattern of good works." A pattern is a model, an example others can copy. Like a dressmaker's pattern or a craftsman's template, it shows others what to do. Titus was a leader, and people would be watching him. His life needed to match his teaching. Paul adds that Titus should show uncorruptness, gravity, and sincerity in his teaching, meaning purity, seriousness, and genuineness. Every one of us is a pattern for someone. Children watch their parents. Younger believers watch older ones. Coworkers notice how we handle pressure. Friends see how we treat others. Whether we realize it or not, we are showing people what faith looks like. That is a sobering thought, but also an opportunity. Our good works can inspire others to do the same. Today, think about who might be watching you. Live in a way that you would be glad for them to copy. Be a pattern of good works.
question: Who is watching your example, and what would you want them to copy?
prayer: Lord, make me a pattern of good works in all things. Help me live today in a way I would be glad for others to follow, for Your sake. Amen.

text: As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith.
reflection: Paul wrote to the Galatians about not growing weary in doing good. Then he added this: "As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith." As we have opportunity. Life is full of chances to do good. Many of them come unexpectedly. A neighbour needs help, a coworker is struggling, a stranger asks for directions. Opportunities are not always convenient, but they are always valuable. And they do not last forever. When an opportunity passes, it may not come again. Paul says do good unto all men. Our kindness should not be limited to people we like or people who are like us. Then he adds, especially unto them who are of the household of faith. Believers are family, and we have a special responsibility to care for one another. But the circle of our kindness extends to everyone. Today, watch for opportunities. When one appears, take it.
question: What opportunity to do good might come your way today, and how could you be ready for it?
prayer: Lord, as I have opportunity, help me do good to all. Open my eyes to the chances You give me today, and let me not let them slip by. Amen.

text: But to do good and to communicate forget not: for with such sacrifices God is well pleased.
reflection: In the Old Testament, worshippers brought animal sacrifices to God. Hebrews explains that Christ's sacrifice fulfilled all of those. But there are still sacrifices that please God. One is praise. And the other is this: "But to do good and to communicate forget not: for with such sacrifices God is well pleased." To communicate here means to share, to give to those in need. Doing good and sharing are sacrifices because they cost us something. Time, money, energy, comfort. And God is well pleased with them. Notice the words forget not. It is easy to forget. Busy schedules, personal needs, and distractions crowd out generosity. We do not mean to be selfish. We simply forget to look beyond ourselves. This verse is a reminder. Every day offers chances to do good and share with others. Each one is an offering that delights God. What sacrifice of goodness can you offer today? Do not forget.
question: What sacrifice of goodness or sharing could you offer God today?
prayer: Lord, to do good and to share are sacrifices that please You. Help me not to forget them, even when they cost me something. Amen.

text: Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy…
reflection: Paul gave Timothy a message for wealthy believers: "Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy." Notice that Paul does not condemn wealth itself. He warns about two dangers that come with it. First, pride: being highminded, thinking we are better because we have more. Second, misplaced trust: relying on riches for security. Riches are uncertain. Markets change. Possessions break. Savings can disappear. But the living God is certain. And notice how Paul describes Him: who giveth us richly all things to enjoy. God is not stingy. He gives generously and wants us to enjoy His gifts. The point is not to despise what we have, but to hold it with open hands and keep our trust in the Giver, not the gifts. By global standards, many of us are rich in this world. Let this charge speak to you today.
question: Where are you tempted to trust in what you have rather than in the God who gives it?
prayer: Lord, keep me from trusting in uncertain riches. You richly give me all things to enjoy. Let my trust rest in You, the Giver, not in the gifts. Amen.

text: That they do good, that they be rich in good works, ready to distribute, willing to communicate…
reflection: Paul continued his instructions for the wealthy with a positive charge: "That they do good, that they be rich in good works, ready to distribute, willing to communicate." Rich in good works. There is a different kind of wealth than money. Some people have little money but are rich in kindness, service, and generosity. Others have great wealth but are poor in good works. Paul wants believers to be rich in what matters most. Ready to distribute means prepared to give, not reluctant. Willing to communicate means eager to share. The next verse explains the result: laying up in store a good foundation against the time to come, that they may lay hold on eternal life. Good works are an investment that lasts. Money spent on ourselves is soon gone. But generosity toward others builds treasure that endures. Whatever your financial situation, you can be rich in good works. Look for ways to share today. Be ready and willing.
question: Whatever your finances, how could you be rich in good works today?
prayer: Lord, make me rich in good works, ready to give and willing to share. Help me lay up treasure that lasts beyond this life. Amen.

text: And if thou draw out thy soul to the hungry, and satisfy the afflicted soul; then shall thy light rise in obscurity, and thy darkness be as the noonday…
reflection: Isaiah 58 addresses people who were fasting and praying but wondering why God did not seem to notice. God answered that their religion was empty. They fasted while mistreating their workers and quarrelling. Then He described the kind of devotion He wanted: caring for the hungry, the oppressed, and the homeless. And He gave a beautiful promise: "if thou draw out thy soul to the hungry, and satisfy the afflicted soul; then shall thy light rise in obscurity, and thy darkness be as the noonday." Draw out thy soul. This is more than handing over food. It is giving yourself, your heart, your compassion. And when we do that, something happens to us. Our own darkness lifts. Light rises in our gloom. Many people find that serving others is one of the best remedies for their own discouragement. When we pour ourselves out for others, God pours light into us. If you feel in the dark today, look for someone to help. Your light may rise as you do.
question: Whom could you help today, and might God lift your own gloom as you do?
prayer: Lord, as I pour myself out for the hungry and afflicted, let my light rise in the darkness. Use my serving to bless others and to lift my own heart. Amen.

text: For the poor shall never cease out of the land: therefore I command thee, saying, Thou shalt open thine hand wide unto thy brother, to thy poor, and to thy needy, in thy land.
reflection: Moses was realistic about the world: "For the poor shall never cease out of the land." There would always be people in need. Rather than seeing this as a reason to give up, Moses saw it as a reason for constant generosity: "therefore I command thee, saying, Thou shalt open thine hand wide unto thy brother, to thy poor, and to thy needy, in thy land." Open thine hand wide. Picture a clenched fist, holding tightly to what it has. Then picture an open hand, ready to give. God commanded His people to live with open hands. Not grudgingly, not partially, but wide open. Poverty is a huge problem, and we cannot solve it alone. But that does not excuse us from helping the people in front of us. Moses mentions thy brother, thy poor, thy needy, in thy land. Start with those near you. Open your hand to someone in need today. Let generosity be a habit, not an occasional event.
question: Who near you is in need, and how could you open your hand to them today?
prayer: Lord, the needs around me are great, but they are no excuse to close my hand. Open my heart and my hand wide to someone in need today. Amen.

text: And he said, He that shewed mercy on him. Then said Jesus unto him, Go, and do thou likewise.
reflection: A lawyer asked Jesus, who is my neighbour? Jesus answered with the story of a man beaten by robbers and left half dead on the road. A priest passed by. A Levite passed by. Then a Samaritan, someone the lawyer would have despised, stopped. He bandaged the man's wounds, put him on his own animal, took him to an inn, and paid for his care. Jesus asked which of the three was a neighbour. The lawyer answered, "He that shewed mercy on him." Then Jesus said, "Go, and do thou likewise." The lawyer wanted to define who deserved his love. Jesus turned the question around. The issue is not who qualifies as my neighbour. It is whether I will be a neighbour to whoever needs me. Mercy does not check credentials. It sees need and responds. Go and do likewise is not a suggestion for later. It is a call to action now. Who needs a neighbour today? Go and show mercy.
question: Who needs you to be a neighbour today, whether or not you think they deserve it?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You told me to go and do likewise. Help me stop asking who deserves my love, and show mercy to whoever needs a neighbour today. Amen.

text: Now there was at Joppa a certain disciple named Tabitha, which by interpretation is called Dorcas: this woman was full of good works and almsdeeds which she did.
reflection: Not much is written about Dorcas in the Bible. But what is written is beautiful: "this woman was full of good works and almsdeeds which she did." She lived in Joppa, and she was known for her kindness, especially to widows. When she died, the widows gathered, weeping, and showed Peter the coats and garments she had made for them. Her life had been spent making clothes for people who could not afford them. Peter prayed, and God raised her back to life. And many in Joppa believed in the Lord. Dorcas was not a preacher or a famous leader. She used a simple skill, sewing, to bless people in need. Her good works were practical, steady, and full of love. Her life left a mark that people could hold in their hands. What simple skill or resource do you have? Cooking, fixing things, listening, organizing, teaching, or driving? Like Dorcas, you can use it to bless others. Let your life be full of good works.
question: What simple skill of yours could you use to bless someone today?
prayer: Lord, Dorcas used a simple skill to bless many. Show me how to use the gifts and skills You have given me to serve someone today. Amen.

text: And the multitude of them that believed were of one heart and of one soul: neither said any of them that ought of the things which he possessed was his own; but they had all things common.
reflection: The early church in Jerusalem was marked by a remarkable spirit of generosity: "the multitude of them that believed were of one heart and of one soul: neither said any of them that ought of the things which he possessed was his own; but they had all things common." This was not a forced arrangement. People gave freely, out of love. They held their possessions loosely. If someone had a need, others met it. The next verses say there was not anyone among them who lacked. And this generosity flowed from unity. They were of one heart and one soul. When people truly love each other, generosity follows naturally. It is hard to hoard when your brother is hungry. This is a challenge for us. How tightly do we hold what we have? Do we see our possessions as ours alone, or as resources God has given us to share? Today, think of one way you could share what you have with someone in need.
question: What do you have that you could hold more loosely and share with someone in need?
prayer: Lord, the early believers were of one heart and shared so that none lacked. Loosen my grip on what I own, and help me share with someone in need. Amen.

text: For ye know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that, though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich.
reflection: When Paul encouraged the Corinthians to give generously, he pointed to the greatest example of generosity there is: "For ye know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that, though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich." Jesus was rich beyond measure. He shared the glory of heaven with the Father. Yet He left it all behind. He was born in humble circumstances, lived without a home of His own, and died with nothing. He became poor. And He did it for your sakes. His poverty made us rich, not necessarily in money, but in forgiveness, relationship with God, eternal life, and every spiritual blessing. This is the foundation of Christian generosity. We do not give because we are told to. We give because we have received so much. When we understand what Christ gave up for us, our own giving becomes a grateful response. Reflect on His generosity today. Let it inspire yours.
question: How could remembering what Christ gave up for you inspire your generosity today?
prayer: Lord Jesus, though You were rich, You became poor for my sake, that I might become rich. Let gratitude for Your generosity make me generous today. Amen.

text: And she went and did according to the saying of Elijah: and she, and he, and her house, did eat many days.
reflection: During a severe drought and famine, God sent the prophet Elijah to a widow in Zarephath. She was gathering sticks to make one last meal for herself and her son before they died of hunger. Elijah asked her to make him a small cake first. It was an enormous request. But Elijah promised that her flour and oil would not run out until the rain returned. The verse tells us what happened: "And she went and did according to the saying of Elijah: and she, and he, and her house, did eat many days." She gave from her last handful, and God provided day after day. The flour never ran out. The oil never failed. This story shows that generosity is not always about giving from abundance. Sometimes it means giving from scarcity, trusting God to provide. The widow's faith was rewarded, not with a single feast, but with daily provision. If you feel you have too little to give, remember her. God can stretch what you offer.
question: What could you offer God today from your little, trusting Him to stretch it?
prayer: Lord, You made the widow's flour and oil last through the famine. Help me trust You when I give from little, knowing You can stretch whatever I offer. Amen.

text: He that hath a bountiful eye shall be blessed; for he giveth of his bread to the poor.
reflection: Proverbs uses an interesting phrase to describe a generous person: "He that hath a bountiful eye shall be blessed; for he giveth of his bread to the poor." A bountiful eye. Generosity begins with how we see. Some people see needs everywhere and respond. Others look right past them. The bountiful eye notices. It sees the lonely person at the edge of the room, the neighbour who is struggling, the coworker who seems discouraged. It looks at others with kindness rather than suspicion. And it leads to action. The bountiful eye does not just notice; it gives. In this verse, it gives bread to the poor, sharing even something as basic as food. And the result is blessing. The generous person is blessed by God. Today, ask God to give you a bountiful eye. Ask Him to help you see people the way He sees them. Then let what you see move you to give.
question: Whose need could you notice today if you looked at them with a bountiful eye?
prayer: Lord, give me a bountiful eye that sees the needs of others with kindness. Help me see people as You see them, and move me to give. Amen.

text: And he said unto them, Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth.
reflection: A man in the crowd asked Jesus to tell his brother to divide the family inheritance with him. Jesus refused to get involved in the dispute. Instead, He addressed the heart issue underneath it: "Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth." Covetousness is the constant desire for more. It is never satisfied. It always wants the next thing. And Jesus warns us to beware of it, because it is subtle. It can creep into anyone's heart, rich or poor. Then He tells a parable about a rich man who built bigger barns to store his crops, planning to take life easy. But that night his life ended, and all his possessions were left behind. Life is not measured by what we own. It is measured by our relationship with God and how we love others. Today, take an honest look at your heart. Where has covetousness crept in? Let it go.
question: Where has the desire for more crept into your heart, and how could you let it go?
prayer: Lord Jesus, my life does not consist in the abundance of the things I possess. Search my heart for covetousness, and teach me to be content in You. Amen.

text: For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.
reflection: Jesus ended His teaching about possessions with a short sentence that reaches deep: "For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also." We often think our hearts direct our money. But Jesus says it also works the other way. Where we put our treasure, our hearts follow. If we invest heavily in earthly things, our hearts become attached to them. If we invest in God's kingdom, through generosity, good works, and care for others, our hearts are drawn toward heaven. This means generosity is not just a result of a changed heart. It is also a way to change our hearts. When we give, our affections shift. We begin to care more about the people and purposes we invest in. This month we have thought about generosity and good works. End it by looking at where your treasure is. Your bank statement and calendar may reveal more than you expect. Then decide where you want your heart to be, and invest your treasure there.
question: Looking at where your treasure goes, where is your heart, and where do you want it to be?
prayer: Lord Jesus, where my treasure is, there my heart will be also. Help me invest my treasure where I want my heart to be, in You and in Your kingdom. Amen.
